You need: one sheet of paper and a clip.

1. Fold the paper over, about as wide as your finger.
2. Turn the paper and fold it back the other way.
3. Keep folding back and forth to the end.
4. Hold the folds together at the base.
5. Put the clip on the base.
6. Open the top. Now you can fan your face!

texts.title: Why Do Cats Purr?
texts.text:
Most people think a cat purrs only when it is happy. Often that is true. A cat curled on a warm lap will purr softly while it is stroked.

But cats also purr at other times. A mother cat purrs to her kittens, which cannot see or hear when they are born. They feel the purr and crawl towards her. Cats sometimes purr when they are hurt or frightened, too. Scientists think the purr may calm the cat down, a little like a child humming to feel brave.

So the next time a cat purrs, look at the rest of it. Is it relaxed and sleepy, or is it hiding under a bed? The purr alone does not tell you everything.

texts.title: Plant a Seed in a Cup
texts.text:
Growing a bean plant

What you need: a paper cup, soil, two bean seeds, water, a pencil.

1. Make a small hole in the base of the cup with the pencil. This lets extra water drain out.
2. Fill the cup with soil, almost to the top.
3. Push the two seeds into the soil, about as deep as the tip of your finger.
4. Water the soil gently until it is damp, not soaking.
5. Put the cup on a sunny window sill.
6. Water a little every two days.

In about a week, a small shoot will push up. If both seeds grow, pull out the weaker one so that the strong one has room.

with a hundred brown arms and a thousand green hands.
Its roots dangle like ropes that swing down to the ground,
and the children climb up without making a sound.

The potter sits beside his wheel
with clay as soft as dough,
he spins it round with patient hands
and shapes it, slow, slow, slow.

A lump becomes a gentle curve,
the curve becomes a pot,
and in the sun it bakes and dries
until it's hard and hot.

Tomorrow in a kitchen far,

Before the stars have gone to bed,

the sea is black, the sky is grey,
and only the moon's half-light afloat.

He throws his net in a silver ring,
he waits, he hums, he watches the tide;
the gulls come screaming overhead
to see what the morning holds inside.

At noon he rows back, tired and slow,
his basket full of flashing fish;
his children run along the sand,
each one is shouting out a wish.

texts.title: The Bridge Made of Roots
texts.text:
In the hills of Meghalaya, in north-east India, some bridges were not built — they were grown.

The Khasi people noticed that the rubber fig tree sends out strong roots above the ground. Over many years, villagers guided these roots across streams, using hollow betel-nut trunks as guides. When the roots reached the other bank, they were allowed to grow into the soil. Slowly, the roots thickened and twisted together into a bridge.

A root bridge can take fifteen years or more to become strong enough to walk on. But once it is grown, it becomes stronger every year, unlike a bridge of wood or steel, which weakens with age. Some root bridges are thought to be hundreds of years old and can carry fifty people at once.

Today, scientists study these bridges as an example of building with nature instead of against it.

texts.text:
Wednesday, 2 October

The power went off at nine this morning and did not come back until the evening. At first it felt like a disaster. No fan, no television, and my phone game died at level eleven.

By lunchtime I had given up being cross. Thatha took out the old carrom board from under his bed. I had never seen him play before, and he beat me three games in a row. He said he used to play by lamplight with his brothers, playing for tamarind seeds.

In the evening we sat on the terrace because the house was hot. We counted fourteen bats and one shooting star. When the lights came back on, everyone cheered, but I was almost sorry.

texts.title: What to Do in an Earthquake
texts.text:
Earthquake safety at school

An earthquake gives no warning, so it helps to know what to do before it happens.

If you are inside:
DROP to the floor, so the shaking cannot knock you over.
COVER your head and neck under a strong desk or table.
HOLD ON to the desk until the shaking stops.

Keep away from windows, shelves and anything that could fall. Do not run outside while the ground is still shaking, and never use a lift.

If you are outside:
Move to an open space, away from buildings, trees and electric wires.

When the shaking stops, follow your teacher calmly to the meeting point on the playground.

texts.title: Make a Rain Gauge
texts.text:
Measure the rain with a rain gauge

You need: a clear plastic bottle, scissors (ask a grown-up), a ruler, tape, and a few pebbles.

1. Ask a grown-up to cut off the top third of the bottle.
2. Put the pebbles in the base, so the bottle does not blow over.
3. Pour in water until it just covers the pebbles. Mark this level as zero.
4. Turn the cut-off top upside down and fit it into the bottle like a funnel. Tape it in place.
5. Tape the ruler to the side, with its zero on your zero mark.
6. Put the gauge in an open place, away from trees and roofs.
7. Check it at the same time each day and write down the level. Then empty it back to zero.

Keep your record for a month and see which week was wettest.

questions.explain: The upside-down top guides rain into the bottle.

past silver ponds and silent towns;
its windows glow like a string of suns
that wander over the darkened downs.

Inside, a baby softly cries,
a grandfather snores, a student reads;
the tea-man calls with sleepy eyes,
"Chai, chai!" to anyone who needs.

At dawn the train will reach the sea,
and all these strangers, side by side,
will step out into the day, set free,
and scatter like seeds far and wide.

texts.text:
The sky was a lid of iron grey,
the air hung heavy, hot and still;
the dogs lay panting in the shade,
the crows were silent on the hill.

Then far away, a drumbeat rolled,
a sudden wind ran through the trees,
and the first plump drops came tumbling down
like coins thrown out by a merchant's sleeve.

The children ran out, faces up,
the farmers laughed beside the plough,
the dry earth breathed a smell so sweet —
and the whole town was singing now.

texts.text:

each morning when the shifts begun.

It carried rice, it carried me,
perched on the bar, my knees held tight;
it carried news from town to town
and Amma's medicine at night.

Now Appa drives a scooter fast,
the bicycle just rusts and waits;
but sometimes, when the house is still,

A garden would teach us things no book can. We could watch seeds grow in science, measure our beds in maths, and write poems about the flowers in English. Our canteen could even cook the spinach we grow.

Some people say a garden is too much work. But each class could look after one small bed, just for twenty minutes a week. If thirty classes share the work, nobody is overloaded.

Please sign the paper outside the office if you agree. With your help, by next summer, the space behind the lab can be green.

Thank you.

texts.title: My Mother's Advice
texts.text:
Adapted from Black Beauty, by Anna Sewell (1877). The story is told by the horse himself.

The first place I can remember was a large, pleasant meadow with a pond of clear water in it. Shady trees leaned over the pond, and rushes and water-lilies grew at the deep end. While I was young I lived on my mother's milk, as I could not eat grass. In the daytime I ran by her side, and at night I lay down close by her.

There were six young colts in the meadow besides me. I used to run with them and have great fun; we would gallop round and round the field as hard as we could go. Sometimes we had rather rough play, for they would often bite and kick as well as gallop.

One day, when there was a good deal of kicking, my mother whinnied to me to come to her, and then she said:

"I wish you to pay attention to what I am going to say to you. The colts who live here are very good colts, but they are cart-horse colts, and of course they have not learned manners. You have been well bred and well born. I hope you will grow up gentle and good, and never learn bad ways. Do your work with a good will, lift your feet up well when you trot, and never bite or kick, even in play."

I have never forgotten my mother's advice. I knew she was a wise old horse, and our master thought a great deal of her.

Faster than fairies, faster than witches,
Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;
And charging along like troops in a battle,
All through the meadows the horses and cattle:
All of the sights of the hill and the plain
Fly as thick as driving rain;
And ever again, in the wink of an eye,
Painted stations whistle by.

Here is a child who clambers and scrambles,
All by himself and gathering brambles;
Here is a tramp who stands and gazes;
And there is the green for stringing the daisies!
Here is a cart run away in the road
Lumping along with man and load;
And here is a mill and there is a river:
Each a glimpse and gone for ever!

texts.title: Mole Meets the River
texts.text:
Adapted from The Wind in the Willows, by Kenneth Grahame (1908).

The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First with brooms, then with dusters, then on ladders and steps and chairs, with a brush and a pail of whitewash, till he had dust in his throat and eyes, and splashes of whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and weary arms. Spring was moving in the air above and in the earth below and around him. It is small wonder, then, that he suddenly flung down his brush on the floor, said "Bother!" and "O blow!" and also "Bother spring-cleaning!" once more and bolted out of the house without even waiting to put on his coat.

He wandered through the meadows, happy and careless, until he stood by the edge of a full-fed river. Never in his life had he seen a river before — this sleek, sinuous, full-bodied animal, chasing and chuckling, gripping things with a gurgle and leaving them with a laugh. All was a-shake and a-shiver: glints and gleams and sparkles, rustle and swirl, chatter and bubble. The Mole was bewitched, entranced, fascinated. He trotted along the side of the river as one trots, when very small, by the side of a man who holds one spellbound by exciting stories; and when tired at last, he sat on the bank, while the river still chattered on to him, a babbling procession of the best stories in the world.

texts.title: Why Do Fireflies Glow?
texts.text:
On warm summer evenings, the fields near rivers sometimes fill with tiny green lights. These are fireflies, small beetles that make their own light.

How do they do it? Inside a firefly's tail, two chemicals mix with oxygen from the air. The reaction gives off light but almost no heat, which is why scientists call it "cold light". A bulb wastes most of its energy as heat; a firefly turns nearly all of its energy into light.

Fireflies glow mainly to find a partner. Each kind of firefly flashes in its own pattern, like a secret code. A male may flash twice and wait; a female of the same kind answers with her own flash.

Sadly, fireflies are becoming rare. Bright street lights confuse their signals, and they lose the damp, dark places where they lay eggs. Turning off outdoor lights at night and keeping some wild grass near ponds can help them return.

texts.title: The Problem with Plastic Straws
texts.text:
Every day, people around the world use hundreds of millions of plastic straws. Most are used for a few minutes and thrown away. Because they are light and small, many slip through recycling machines and end up in rivers and seas.

In the sea, plastic does not rot. Sunlight and waves break it into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics. Fish and seabirds swallow these pieces, mistaking them for food. Scientists have found microplastics in the stomachs of turtles, in sea salt and even in drinking water.

Some cities have banned plastic straws. Cafes now offer paper, steel or bamboo straws instead, or simply no straw at all. Critics point out that straws are only a tiny part of all ocean plastic, and that some people with disabilities need bendy plastic straws to drink safely.

Still, supporters say the ban is a useful first step. Refusing a straw is easy, and it makes people think about all the other plastic they use only once.

texts.title: The Night of the Cyclone
texts.text:
Thursday, 12 December, 11 pm

The wind has been roaring since dinner. The radio says the cyclone will cross the coast near us tonight. Appa has nailed boards over the big windows, and we have filled every bucket with water in case the taps stop.

The lights went out at nine. Now we are sitting in the middle room with two candles, the radio and a packet of biscuits. Every few minutes something bangs against the roof — a branch, maybe, or a neighbour's tin sheet. Paati is whispering softly to herself. My little brother fell asleep on my lap, which is amazing, because I could not sleep if you paid me.

Friday, 7 am

It is over. The street looks like a giant has walked through it: trees lying across the road, wires down, the tea stall's roof in our garden. But everyone on our lane is safe. Appa and the neighbours are already clearing the road with saws. I am making tea for everybody on the gas stove.

He comes each January, thin and brown,
with a hundred kites tied above his head,
a rainbow walking through the town,
yellow, purple, green and red.

The children follow, three and four,
like ducklings in a crooked line;
they count their coins, then count once more,
and point and whisper, "That one's mine."

He never flies a kite himself;
his hands are busy, his eyes are old.
He sells the sky, then counts his wealth:
a few warm coins against the cold.

And when the last kite leaves his hand
and climbs into the windy blue,
he smiles as if he understands
a kind of flying, too.

Each night she climbs the ninety stairs,
a lantern swinging from her hand,
to where the great glass eye looks out
across the dark and sleeping land.

She trims the wick, she cleans the glass,
she listens to the ocean roar;
she counts the ships by their small lights
like candles on a moving floor.

The sailors never know her name,
they only know the steady beam
that keeps them safe from hidden rocks
and guides them homeward, like a dream.

And in the morning, tired and pale,
she walks the ninety stairs once more,
and sleeps, while all the fishing boats
come laughing in to reach the shore.

texts.text:
The little blue train to Ooty does not rush. It climbs. For five hours it pushes and puffs up the Nilgiri hills, so slowly that in places you could step off, pick a flower and step back on.

We left Mettupalayam in warm sunshine, past banana fields and areca palms. Within an hour the air grew cool, and the plants changed: ferns hung over the line, and the first tea gardens appeared, neat green rows combed across the slopes.

The train crossed more than two hundred bridges and passed through sixteen tunnels. Each time we entered one, the children in our carriage screamed with delight, and each time we came out, the view was different — a waterfall, a valley full of mist, a village with roofs like scattered playing cards.

By the time we reached Ooty, I was wearing my sweater and holding a cup of hot tea. It felt as though we had travelled not just up a mountain, but into a different season.

texts.title: A Mad Tea-Party
texts.text:
Adapted from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, by Lewis Carroll (1865).

There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it. A Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep. The table was a large one, but the three were all crowded together at one corner of it.

"No room! No room!" they cried out when they saw Alice coming.

"There's plenty of room!" said Alice indignantly, and she sat down in a large arm-chair at one end of the table.

"Have some cake," the March Hare said in an encouraging tone.

Alice looked all round the table, but there was nothing on it but tea. "I don't see any cake," she remarked.

"There isn't any," said the March Hare.

"Then it wasn't very civil of you to offer it," said Alice angrily.

"It wasn't very civil of you to sit down without being invited," said the March Hare.

The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was, "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?"

"Come, we shall have some fun now!" thought Alice. "I'm glad they've begun asking riddles. I believe I can guess that," she added aloud.

"Do you mean that you think you can find out the answer to it?" said the March Hare.

"Exactly so," said Alice.

"Then you should say what you mean," the March Hare went on.

"I do," Alice hastily replied; "at least — at least I mean what I say — that's the same thing, you know."

"Not the same thing a bit!" said the Hatter. "You might just as well say that 'I see what I eat' is the same thing as 'I eat what I see'!"

texts.title: Daffodils
texts.text:
by William Wordsworth (1807)

I wandered lonely as a cloud
That floats on high o'er vales and hills,
When all at once I saw a crowd,
A host, of golden daffodils;
Beside the lake, beneath the trees,
Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.

Continuous as the stars that shine
And twinkle on the milky way,
They stretched in never-ending line
Along the margin of a bay:
Ten thousand saw I at a glance,
Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.

The waves beside them danced; but they
Out-did the sparkling waves in glee:
A poet could not but be gay,
In such a jocund company:
I gazed — and gazed — but little thought
What wealth the show to me had brought:

For oft, when on my couch I lie
In vacant or in pensive mood,
They flash upon that inward eye
Which is the bliss of solitude;
And then my heart with pleasure fills,
And dances with the daffodils.

texts.title: Gulliver Wakes in Lilliput
texts.text:
Adapted from Gulliver's Travels, by Jonathan Swift (1726). Gulliver, a ship's doctor, has swum ashore after a shipwreck and fallen asleep on the grass.

When I woke, it was just daylight. I tried to rise, but was not able to stir. As I happened to lie on my back, I found my arms and legs were strongly fastened on each side to the ground, and my hair, which was long and thick, tied down in the same manner. I likewise felt several slender ropes across my body, from my armpits to my thighs. I could only look upwards; the sun began to grow hot, and the light hurt my eyes.

I heard a confused noise about me, but in the posture I lay, could see nothing except the sky. In a little time I felt something alive moving on my left leg, which, advancing gently forward over my chest, came almost up to my chin. Bending my eyes downward as much as I could, I saw it to be a human creature not six inches high, with a bow and arrow in his hands and a quiver at his back. In the meantime I felt at least forty more of the same kind following the first.

I was in the utmost astonishment, and roared so loud that they all ran back in a fright; and some of them, as I was afterwards told, were hurt by the falls they got by leaping from my sides upon the ground. However, they soon returned, and one of them, who ventured so far as to get a full sight of my face, lifting up his hands and eyes by way of admiration, cried out in a shrill but distinct voice words I could not understand.

texts.title: The Man's Cub
texts.text:
Adapted from "Mowgli's Brothers" in The Jungle Book, by Rudyard Kipling (1894).

It was seven o'clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day's rest, scratched himself, yawned, and spread out his paws one after the other to get rid of the sleepy feeling in their tips. Mother Wolf lay with her big grey nose dropped across her four tumbling, squealing cubs, and the moon shone into the mouth of the cave where they all lived.

Suddenly Father Wolf heard something coming uphill through the bushes. He crouched, ready to spring. Then he stopped himself in mid-air.

"Man!" he snapped. "A man's cub. Look!"

Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a little brown baby who could just walk — as soft and as dimpled a little thing as ever came to a wolf's cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf's face and laughed.

"Is that a man's cub?" said Mother Wolf. "I have never seen one. Bring it here."

Father Wolf carried the baby gently in his mouth and set it down among the cubs, without a single tooth even scratching the skin. The little one pushed his way between the cubs to get close to the warm fur.

"How little! How bold!" said Mother Wolf softly. "He is eating his food with the others. And so this is a man's cub. Was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man's cub among her children?"

Outside, the great tiger Shere Khan was roaring at the mouth of the cave, angry that the child had escaped him. But Mother Wolf looked at the baby and said, "Lie still, little frog. O thou Mowgli — for Mowgli the Frog I will call thee — the time will come when thou wilt hunt Shere Khan as he has hunted thee."

texts.title: Christmas Won't Be Christmas
texts.text:
Adapted from Little Women, by Louisa May Alcott (1868). The four March sisters are poor, and their father is away.

"Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents," grumbled Jo, lying on the rug.

"It's so dreadful to be poor!" sighed Meg, looking down at her old dress.

"I don't think it's fair for some girls to have plenty of pretty things, and other girls nothing at all," added little Amy, with an injured sniff.

"We've got Father and Mother, and each other," said Beth contentedly from her corner.

The four young faces on which the firelight shone brightened at the cheerful words, but darkened again as Jo said sadly, "We haven't got Father, and shall not have him for a long time." She didn't say "perhaps never", but each silently added it, thinking of Father far away.

Nobody spoke for a minute; then Meg said in an altered tone, "You know the reason Mother proposed not having any presents this Christmas was because it is going to be a hard winter for everyone, and she thinks we ought not to spend money for pleasure. We can't do much, but we can make our little sacrifices, and ought to do it gladly."

Each girl had a dollar of her own, and each had been planning to spend it on herself: a book for Jo, music for Beth, drawing pencils for Amy. Then Beth looked at Mother's old slippers warming by the fire. "Mother's shoes are quite worn out," she said softly. "I'll tell you what we'll do," said Jo, sitting up. "Let's each get her something for Christmas, and not get anything for ourselves."

texts.text:
Adapted from Oliver Twist, by Charles Dickens (1838). Oliver is a nine-year-old orphan in a workhouse, where poor children are given very little to eat.

The room in which the boys were fed was a large stone hall, with a copper at one end, out of which the master, dressed in an apron for the purpose, ladled the gruel at meal-times. Of this thin porridge each boy had one small bowl, and no more — except on festive occasions, when he had two ounces and a quarter of bread besides.

The bowls never wanted washing. The boys polished them with their spoons till they shone again; and when they had done this, they would sit staring at the copper with such eager eyes, as if they could have devoured the very bricks of which it was composed.

Oliver Twist and his companions suffered the tortures of slow hunger for three months. At last they held a council. Lots were cast who should walk up to the master after supper that evening and ask for more; and it fell to Oliver Twist.

The evening arrived; the boys took their places. The gruel was served out, and disappeared. The boys whispered to each other and winked at Oliver, while his next neighbours nudged him. Child as he was, he was desperate with hunger. He rose from the table, and advancing to the master, basin and spoon in hand, said, somewhat alarmed at his own boldness:

"Please, sir, I want some more."

The master was a stout, healthy man, but he turned very pale. He gazed in stupefied astonishment on the small rebel for some seconds. The assistants were paralysed with wonder; the boys with fear.

"What!" said the master at length, in a faint voice.

"Please, sir," replied Oliver, "I want some more."

texts.title: The Old Sea-Dog at the Admiral Benbow
texts.text:
Adapted from Treasure Island, by Robert Louis Stevenson (1883). Jim Hawkins, a boy whose parents keep an inn by the sea, tells the story.

I remember him as if it were yesterday, as he came plodding to the inn door, his sea-chest following behind him in a hand-barrow — a tall, strong, heavy, nut-brown man, his tarry pigtail falling over the shoulder of his soiled blue coat, his hands ragged and scarred, with black, broken nails, and the sabre cut across one cheek, a dirty, livid white. I remember him looking round the cove and whistling to himself as he did so, and then breaking out in that old sea-song that he sang so often afterwards: "Fifteen men on the dead man's chest — Yo-ho-ho!"

He was a very silent man by custom. All day he hung round the cove or upon the cliffs with a brass telescope; all evening he sat in a corner of the parlour next the fire. Every day when he came back from his stroll he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the road. At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind that made him ask; but at last we began to see he was desirous to avoid them.

He had taken me aside one day and promised me a silver coin on the first of every month if I would only keep my "weather-eye open for a seafaring man with one leg" and let him know the moment he appeared. How that personage haunted my dreams, I need scarcely tell you. On stormy nights, when the wind shook the four corners of the house, I would see him in a thousand forms, and with a thousand fiendish expressions.

texts.title: The Myth of the Five-Second Rule
texts.text:
Many children believe in the "five-second rule": if food falls on the floor, it is safe to eat as long as you pick it up within five seconds. It is a comforting idea, but is it true?

In 2016, scientists in the United States tested it. They dropped watermelon, bread, buttered bread and sweets onto steel, tiles, wood and carpet that had been covered with harmless bacteria. They then measured how many bacteria moved onto the food after less than one second, five seconds, thirty seconds and five minutes.

The results were clear. Bacteria jumped onto food in less than one second. Longer times did mean more bacteria, but there was no safe moment. Wet food, such as watermelon, picked up the most, because bacteria travel easily in moisture. Surprisingly, carpet passed fewer bacteria than tiles or steel, perhaps because food touches less of its surface.

The researchers' conclusion was simple: the five-second rule is "a significant oversimplification". In other words, it may make us feel better, but it does not keep us safe.

texts.text:
The Editor
The Morning Chronicle
Coimbatore

Sir,

I am a Class 8 student who cycles six kilometres to school every day. I am writing about the dangerous junction at Gandhi Road and Mill Street.

Every morning, about two hundred children cross this junction. There is no zebra crossing, no traffic signal and no policeman. Buses turn without slowing down. Last month a classmate of mine was knocked off his bicycle; luckily he escaped with a broken wrist.

I have spoken to my teachers and to other parents, and we all agree that a simple traffic signal and a painted crossing would make the junction much safer. A crossing guard during school hours would help even more.

I hope that, by printing this letter, your newspaper will bring this problem to the attention of the authorities before a more serious accident happens.

Yours faithfully,
Karthik R.
Class 8, Valley Public School

texts.title: The Last Tiger Speaks
texts.text:
Once I was the forest's quiet fire:
my stripes were sunlight falling through the reeds,
my footsteps were the silence before rain.
The deer knew me as they know the wind —
not seen, but felt along the skin.

Now the forest is a narrow room.
Roads run like scars across my sleeping ground,
and every year the walls grow closer in.
I smell your smoke at night; I hear your trucks;
I drink from rivers that taste of iron.

Do not paint me on your walls and coins
and leave my cubs no place to learn the hunt.
A tiger on a flag is only cloth.
Give me the forest back, and I will be
your living flag, burning in the green.

texts.text:
My grandmother's house had two doors.
The front one was for guests and priests,
painted green, with a brass lion
who held a ring between his teeth.

The back one opened on the well,
on hens and ash and drying chillies,
on the washerwoman's songs
and the neighbour's goat, and the lilies.

Guests saw the lion and the green;
they sat on cushions, drank from glass.
But all of us who were family
came round the back, across the grass.

And now, whenever I visit someone,
I wonder, as I ring their bell,
whether I am a front-door person
or one who knows the well.

texts.title: School Report: The Water Audit
texts.text:
WATER AUDIT REPORT — CLASS 7B
Prepared for the Principal, October

Aim
To find out how much water our school wastes and suggest ways to save it.

Method
For one week, groups of four pupils checked every tap, toilet and the garden hose twice a day. We timed leaks with a stopwatch and measured how fast a bucket filled.

Findings
• 9 of our 42 taps leak. Together they waste about 380 litres a day.
• Two toilet cisterns run all the time, wasting about 600 litres a day.
• The garden hose is left on for about 40 minutes after watering, wasting about 500 litres a day.
• In total, roughly 1,500 litres a day are wasted — enough to fill 75 large buckets.

Recommendations
1. Repair the leaking taps and cisterns (estimated cost: 6,000 rupees).
2. Fit a timer on the garden hose.
3. Put "Close the tap" reminders above sinks.

Conclusion
Most of the waste comes from a few faults that are cheap to repair. Fixing them would pay for itself within a few months in lower water bills.

Good morning, teachers and friends.

Last week, I counted the lights and fans left on in empty classrooms during lunch. In one break alone, I found twenty-three fans and forty lights running with nobody in the room. That is like leaving a tap open while you go on holiday.

Some of you will say, "One fan does not matter." Perhaps not. But our school has thirty-two classrooms. If each wastes just one hour of electricity a day, that adds up to thousands of rupees in a year — money that could buy books for our library, or new nets for the football field.

So I have one small request. Let us choose a "Switch Monitor" in every class. Before the room is empty, the monitor checks that every switch is off. It takes ten seconds. It costs nothing.

Our planet is not something we inherit from our parents; it is something we borrow from our children. Let's start paying it back, one switch at a time.

Thank you.

texts.title: Hampi at Sunrise
texts.text:
We climbed Matanga Hill in the dark, our torches making small yellow circles on the rock. The path was steep and uneven, and twice I had to use my hands. By the time we reached the top, my legs were shaking and the sky in the east had turned from black to a deep, bruised purple.

Then the sun came up, and Hampi appeared below us as if someone were slowly lifting a cloth from a table. First the tops of the boulders caught the light, enormous rounded stones piled on one another like a giant's abandoned game of marbles. Then the ruins appeared between them: the long market street, broken pillars, a stepped tank, the great gateway tower standing above the palm trees.

Five hundred years ago, this was one of the largest cities in the world, the capital of the Vijayanagara empire, with markets selling horses, pearls and silk. Now a langur sat on the wall beside me, eating a biscuit it had certainly not been given.

On the way down, our guide said that Hampi was destroyed in a single season of war, but took two centuries to build. I thought about that all the way back to the bus.

texts.title: Scrooge
texts.text:
Adapted from A Christmas Carol, by Charles Dickens (1843).

Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! A squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster. The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, made his eyes red and his thin lips blue. He carried his own low temperature always about with him; he iced his office in the summer, and did not thaw it one degree at Christmas.

Nobody ever stopped him in the street to say, with gladsome looks, "My dear Scrooge, how are you? When will you come to see me?" No children asked him what it was o'clock. Even the blind men's dogs appeared to know him, and when they saw him coming on, would tug their owners into doorways.

Once upon a time — of all the good days in the year, on Christmas Eve — old Scrooge sat busy in his counting-house. It was cold, bleak, biting weather, and the fog came pouring in at every chink and keyhole. The door of Scrooge's office was open, so that he might keep his eye upon his clerk, Bob Cratchit, who in a dismal little cell beyond was copying letters. Scrooge had a very small fire, but the clerk's fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal. He could not replenish it, for Scrooge kept the coal-box in his own room.

"A merry Christmas, uncle!" cried a cheerful voice. It was Scrooge's nephew, who came in glowing with the cold and the rapid walk.

"Bah!" said Scrooge. "Humbug!"

"Christmas a humbug, uncle! You don't mean that, I am sure?"

"I do," said Scrooge. "Merry Christmas! What right have you to be merry? You're poor enough."

texts.title: The Footprint
texts.text:
Adapted from Robinson Crusoe, by Daniel Defoe (1719). Crusoe has lived alone on an island for many years, believing nobody else ever comes there.

It happened one day, about noon, going towards my boat, I was exceedingly surprised with the print of a man's bare foot on the shore, which was very plain to be seen in the sand. I stood like one thunderstruck, or as if I had seen a ghost. I listened, I looked round me, but I could hear nothing, nor see anything. I went up to a rising ground to look farther. I went up the shore and down the shore, but it was all one; I could see no other impression but that one. I went to it again to see if there were any more, and to observe if it might not be my fancy; but there was no room for that, for there was exactly the very print of a foot — toes, heel, and every part of a foot. How it came thither I knew not, nor could in the least imagine.

After innumerable fluttering thoughts, like a man perfectly confused and out of myself, I came home to my fortification, not feeling, as we say, the ground I went on, but terrified to the last degree, looking behind me at every two or three steps, mistaking every bush and tree, and fancying every stump at a distance to be a man.

Nor is it possible to describe how many various shapes my frightened imagination represented things to me in; how many wild ideas were found every moment in my fancy, and what strange thoughts came into my head by the way.

When I came to my castle, for so I think I called it ever after this, I fled into it like one pursued. I slept none that night. The farther I was from the occasion of my fright, the greater my fears were — which is something contrary to the nature of such things.

questions.prompt: Why is one footprint so frightening to Crusoe?
questions.right: He thought he was alone on the island
wrong: He is very afraid of the sea
The print was enormous in size
questions.explain: After years alone, it means someone else has come.

questions.prompt: What does "I stood like one thunderstruck" mean?
questions.explain: Thunderstruck means too shocked to move.

questions.prompt: What did he check when he went back to the print?
questions.right: Whether there were more prints or he had imagined it
wrong: Whether the tide had washed it away
Whether it matched his own boots
questions.explain: He looked for more and checked it was not "my fancy".

questions.prompt: How does telling the story in the first person help here?
questions.right: We share his panic from inside his mind
wrong: We learn who made the footprint
We see the island from the sky
questions.explain: His racing thoughts and fears are told directly.

questions.prompt: What does "fancying every stump at a distance to be a man" show?
questions.right: Fear was making him imagine danger everywhere
wrong: There were many men hiding nearby
His eyesight had become very poor
questions.explain: His frightened imagination turns ordinary things into threats.

questions.prompt: What is unusual about his fear, as he says at the end?
questions.right: It grew stronger the farther he was from the print
wrong: It vanished as soon as he was home
He laughed about it the next day
questions.explain: "The farther I was… the greater my fears were."

texts.title: Natasha's Dance
texts.text:
Adapted from War and Peace, by Leo Tolstoy (1869), translated from Russian. Natasha, a young countess brought up in a grand house in Moscow by a French governess, visits her old uncle in his simple country home after a day's hunting.

The uncle took down his guitar, blew the dust off it, and, tapping the lid with his fingers, tuned it and settled himself in his chair. He took the guitar a little above the neck, winked at Natasha, and began to play a lively Russian dance tune.

Natasha listened, her face glowing. "Uncle, darling! More, more!" she cried, as soon as he had finished. She jumped up and threw her arms round him and kissed him.

"Now, little niece!" he said, waving his hand. "Your turn!" And he struck up the tune again.

Natasha threw off the shawl from her shoulders, ran forward to face her uncle, set her arms on her hips, made a motion with her shoulders, and stood still.

Where, how and when had this young countess, educated by a French governess, picked up from the Russian air she breathed the spirit of that dance? Where had she learnt those movements, which should have been driven out long ago by the dancing lessons of the city? Yet the spirit and the movements were exactly those that her uncle had expected. As soon as she had struck her pose and smiled a triumphant, proud and cunning smile, the fear that had seized everyone in the room — that she might not do it right — was gone, and they were already admiring her.

She did the right thing with such precision, such complete precision, that Anisya, the housekeeper, who had handed her the shawl, had tears in her eyes, though she laughed as she watched this slim, graceful countess, reared in silks and velvet, so different from herself, who yet understood all that was in Anisya, and in Anisya's father, and mother, and aunt, and in every Russian man and woman.

questions.prompt: Who had taught Natasha as a child?
questions.explain: She was "educated by a French governess".

questions.prompt: Why were people afraid before she danced?
questions.right: A city countess might not know the dance
wrong: Her uncle played the guitar badly
questions.explain: She was raised with city dancing lessons, not country dances.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator ask "Where, how and when" she learnt the dance?
questions.right: To wonder at how she knew it without being taught
wrong: Because the narrator does not care
questions.explain: The questions show surprise at her natural understanding.

questions.prompt: What does the dance show about Natasha?
questions.right: She shares a deep bond with ordinary Russian people
wrong: She wants to leave Russia for France
She dislikes her uncle's country home
questions.explain: She understands what is in Anisya and "every Russian man and woman".

questions.prompt: Why did Anisya laugh and cry at the same time?
wrong: She was hurt by the shawl
questions.explain: She was touched that a countess so different from her understood her world.

questions.prompt: What does "precision" mean here?
questions.explain: She did each movement exactly right.

texts.title: You Have Been in Afghanistan
texts.text:
Adapted from A Study in Scarlet, by Arthur Conan Doyle (1887). Dr Watson has just met Sherlock Holmes, who greeted him with: "You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive." Later Watson asks how Holmes knew.

"You appeared to be surprised when I told you, on our first meeting, that you had come from Afghanistan."

"You were told, no doubt."

"Nothing of the sort. I knew you came from Afghanistan. From long habit the train of thoughts ran so swiftly through my mind that I arrived at the conclusion without being conscious of the steps between. There were such steps, however. The train of reasoning ran: 'Here is a gentleman of a medical type, but with the air of a military man. Clearly an army doctor, then. He has just come from the tropics, for his face is dark, and that is not the natural colour of his skin, for his wrists are fair. He has undergone hardship and sickness, as his tired face says clearly. His left arm has been injured: he holds it in a stiff and unnatural manner. Where in the tropics could an English army doctor have seen much hardship and got his arm hurt? Clearly in Afghanistan.' The whole train of thought did not occupy a second. I then remarked that you came from Afghanistan, and you were astonished."

"It is simple enough as you explain it," I said, smiling.

Holmes looked a little put out. "That is the way with all explanations," he said. "Once you see how a thing is done, it seems obvious. But observing is not the same as seeing. You see, Watson, but you do not observe. The difference is clear. For example, you have often seen the steps which lead up from the hall to this room."

"Frequently."

"How often?"

"Well, some hundreds of times."

"Then how many are there?"

"How many? I don't know."

"Quite so! You have not observed. And yet you have seen. That is just my point. Now, I know that there are seventeen steps, because I have both seen and observed."

questions.prompt: How did Holmes know Watson had been in the tropics?
questions.right: His face was tanned but his wrists were pale
wrong: Watson had told him so before
questions.explain: Dark face, fair wrists: the tan came from a hot country.

questions.prompt: Which clue told Holmes that Watson was an army doctor?
questions.right: He looked medical but had a military air
wrong: His left arm was held stiffly
questions.explain: A medical type with a military air must be an army doctor.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between seeing and observing, according to Holmes?
questions.right: Observing means noticing and remembering details
wrong: Seeing is something done with glasses
There is no real difference at all
questions.explain: Watson has seen the steps hundreds of times but cannot say how many.

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes look "a little put out"?
wrong: He has hurt his arm again
He has lost count of the steps
questions.explain: Watson says it is "simple enough", which annoys him.

questions.prompt: Why does Holmes use the example of the steps?
questions.right: To prove his point with something Watson knows
wrong: To ask Watson to count them now
To show the house is old
questions.explain: It shows plainly that Watson has seen without observing.

questions.prompt: What does "perceive" mean in "I perceive"?
questions.explain: Holmes means he can tell from what he notices.

texts.title: Where the Mind Is Without Fear

questions.prompt: How is the poem built?
questions.right: A list of "Where…" lines leading to one wish
questions.explain: Each line begins "Where", and the last line gives the wish.

questions.prompt: What are "narrow domestic walls"?
wrong: The walls of a very small house
questions.explain: They break the world "into fragments": they divide people.

questions.prompt: What does "the dreary desert sand of dead habit" stand for?
questions.right: Thinking that has dried up through old habits
wrong: A real desert somewhere in India
The sand on a sunny beach
questions.explain: Reason, like a stream, can be lost in habit, like water in sand.

questions.prompt: What does the poet wish for his country?
questions.right: A free, truthful and thoughtful nation
wrong: A return to the old ways
questions.explain: "Into that heaven of freedom… let my country awake."

questions.prompt: What does "striving" mean?
questions.explain: Tireless striving: working hard without stopping.

texts.title: The Old Oak
texts.text:
Adapted from War and Peace, by Leo Tolstoy (1869), translated from Russian. Prince Andrei, tired and unhappy after years of war and loss, is travelling through the countryside in spring.

At the edge of the road stood an oak. It was probably ten times the age of the birches that formed the wood, ten times as thick and twice as tall as any of them. It was an enormous tree, with branches broken long ago and bark scarred with old wounds. With its huge, crooked, gnarled arms and fingers stretched out, it stood like an old, angry, scornful monster among the smiling birches. It alone would not yield to the spring. It did not want to see the sun or feel the warm wind.

"Spring, and love, and happiness!" this oak seemed to say. "Aren't you tired of that same tired, senseless trick? It is always the same, and always a lie. There is no spring, no sun, no happiness."

"Yes, the oak is right, a thousand times right," thought Prince Andrei. "Let others, the young, give in to that trick again, but we know life. Our life is finished."

Six weeks later, in June, he drove home along the same road. He looked for the old oak, and did not recognise it at first. The old oak, quite changed, spread out a tent of dark, juicy green, and seemed to sway gently in the evening sun. There were no crooked fingers now, no scars, no old distrust and grief. Through the rough bark, young leaves had pushed out, so fresh that it was hard to believe the old tree had grown them.

"Yes, it is the same oak," thought Prince Andrei, and a sudden, unreasoning feeling of joy and renewal came over him. All the best moments of his life came back to him at once. "No, life is not over," he decided suddenly and for good. "It is not enough for me to know what is in me. Everyone must know it."

questions.prompt: In spring, the oak is described like "an old, angry, scornful monster". Why?
questions.right: It seems to refuse the spring like a bitter person
wrong: It is about to fall across the road
Wild animals are living inside it
questions.explain: Its bare, twisted branches seem to reject the spring around it.

questions.prompt: Why does Prince Andrei agree with the oak at first?
questions.right: He feels his own life is finished
wrong: He wants to cut it down
questions.explain: "Our life is finished." He sees himself in the tree.

questions.prompt: How has the oak changed by June?
questions.right: It is covered in fresh green leaves
wrong: It has lost all its branches
questions.explain: "Spread out a tent of dark, juicy green."

questions.prompt: What does the oak stand for in this extract?
questions.right: Prince Andrei's own feelings about life
questions.explain: Its gloom matches his in spring; its new leaves match his new hope.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer show the oak twice, weeks apart?
questions.right: To mirror the change in Prince Andrei
wrong: To show how slowly trees grow
questions.explain: The tree's change and his change happen together.

questions.prompt: How does Prince Andrei feel at the end?
questions.right: full of sudden joy and hope
questions.explain: "A sudden, unreasoning feeling of joy and renewal."

texts.title: The Postmaster
texts.text:
Adapted from "The Postmaster", a story by Rabindranath Tagore (1891), translated from Bengali.

The postmaster first took up his duties in the village of Ulapur. Though the village was a small one, there was an indigo factory near by, and its owner had managed to get a post office opened. Our postmaster was a young man from Calcutta. He felt like a fish out of water in this remote village. His office and living room were in a dark thatched shed, not far from a green, slimy pond surrounded by thick jungle.

His salary was small. He had to cook his own meals, which were served to him by Ratan, an orphan girl of the village, who did odd jobs for him for a small payment. She was about twelve years old.

In the evenings, when the smoke began to curl up from the village cowsheds and the crickets chirped in every bush, the postmaster would sit outside, and sometimes he would call Ratan and talk. He told her about his mother and his elder sister at home, about the family he missed so much. Ratan listened, and soon she spoke of "his mother" and "his sister" as if she had always known them. In return, the postmaster began to teach her the alphabet, and she learnt quickly.

Then one day, after weeks of rain, the postmaster fell ill with fever. Ratan stayed by his side day and night. She brought him medicine, cooled his forehead with her hand and would not leave him for a moment. When at last he recovered, he decided he had had enough of this village and asked to be transferred. His request was refused, and he resigned.

"Ratan, I am going away tomorrow," he said that evening.

"Will you take me home with you?" she asked.

The postmaster laughed. "What an idea!" he said, and he did not explain.

The next morning, as the boat carried him down the swollen river, a pain gripped his heart. He thought of the little village girl and wished he could go back for her. But the wind filled the sail, and the village slipped away behind the bend. Ratan, meanwhile, wandered about the post office, hoping, in the stubborn way of the human heart, that he might still return.

questions.prompt: What does "like a fish out of water" tell us about the postmaster?
questions.right: He felt uncomfortable and out of place
wrong: He liked swimming in the pond
questions.explain: A city man in a remote village does not feel at home.

questions.prompt: Why did Ratan speak of "his mother" and "his sister" as if she knew them?
questions.right: She had grown close to him and his stories
wrong: She had met them in Calcutta
questions.explain: Listening every evening, his family became real to her.

questions.prompt: What does Ratan's care during his illness show?
wrong: Her wish to be paid more
questions.explain: She stayed day and night and would not leave him.

questions.prompt: Why does the postmaster laugh at Ratan's question?
questions.right: He has not thought of her as family
wrong: He plans to come back for her
questions.explain: To him it seems an odd idea, though she is serious.

questions.prompt: What is the main feeling at the end of the story?
questions.right: Sadness at a bond that only one fully valued
wrong: Joy at going home to Calcutta
Anger at the people of the village
questions.explain: He feels a passing pain; she keeps hoping he will return.

questions.prompt: Why does the story end with Ratan, not the postmaster?
questions.right: To leave the reader with her quiet hope and loss
wrong: To introduce a new postmaster to readers
To explain how the indigo factory works
questions.explain: The last image is of her waiting, which stays with the reader.

texts.title: A Truth Universally Acknowledged
texts.text:
Adapted from Pride and Prejudice, by Jane Austen (1813).

It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families that he is considered the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.

"My dear Mr Bennet," said his lady to him one day, "have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?"

Mr Bennet replied that he had not.

"But it is," returned she; "for Mrs Long has just been here, and she told me all about it."

Mr Bennet made no answer.

"Do you not want to know who has taken it?" cried his wife impatiently.

"You want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it."

This was invitation enough.

"Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs Long says that Netherfield is taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England. His name is Bingley, and he is single, my dear! What a fine thing for our girls!"

"How so? How can it affect them?"

"My dear Mr Bennet," replied his wife, "how can you be so tiresome! You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them."

"Is that his plan in settling here?"

"Plan! Nonsense, how can you talk so! But it is very likely that he may fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as soon as he comes."

questions.prompt: The first sentence says something is "universally acknowledged". Is the writer serious?
questions.right: No, she is gently mocking what families believe
wrong: Yes, it is a scientific fact
Yes, every rich man wants a wife
questions.explain: The next sentence shows it is really the neighbours' wish, not the man's.

questions.prompt: What does Mr Bennet's "I have no objection to hearing it" show?
questions.right: He is teasing his wife with dry humour
wrong: He is very excited about the news
He has not heard what she said
questions.explain: He knows she longs to tell him, and replies coolly.

questions.prompt: How is Mrs Bennet shown?
questions.right: eager and impatient to marry off her daughters
wrong: shy and quiet with her husband
questions.explain: She rushes to tell the news and plans a marriage at once.

questions.prompt: In this extract, what does "a good fortune" mean?
questions.explain: A man of "large fortune" is rich.

questions.prompt: How does the writer create humour in the conversation?
questions.right: By contrasting Mrs Bennet's excitement with Mr Bennet's calm replies
wrong: By having the characters tell jokes in a list
By describing their funny clothes in detail
questions.explain: Her eager speeches meet his short, dry answers.

questions.prompt: Whose view does the opening sentence really give?
questions.explain: It is "well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families".

texts.title: The Girl Who Mapped the Stars
texts.text:
In 1890s Madras, few people expected a girl to become a scientist. Kamala, the daughter of a clerk at the observatory, was expected to learn music and marry young. Instead, she spent her evenings on the observatory roof with her father, learning the names of the stars in Tamil, English and Latin. (Kamala is a character invented for this text, though many real women of the time faced the same barriers.)

Her father noticed her talent before anyone else. When she was twelve, he gave her an old notebook from the observatory and asked her to copy the nightly positions of Jupiter's moons. She did more than copy. Within a year she had spotted two mistakes in the printed tables the observatory relied on, and she had worked out why: the astronomer who wrote them had used the wrong date for a change in the calendar.

The director of the observatory refused at first to believe that a child had found the errors. He checked her working himself — and then, to his credit, published a correction with a note thanking "a young assistant". He did not print her name.

Kamala went on to calculate tables for the observatory for thirty years, always as an "assistant", always paid less than the men she trained. Late in life she wrote: "I did not need my name on the tables. I needed the tables to be right. But I should have liked the girls after me to see that a name like mine could be there."

Today, historians are finding many such hidden workers in the records of science. Their names were left out, but their numbers are still in the books.

questions.prompt: What did Kamala find in the printed tables?
questions.right: Two mistakes caused by a wrong date
wrong: A new moon going round Jupiter
A star with its name missing
questions.explain: She spotted two mistakes; the writer had used the wrong date for a calendar change.

questions.prompt: What does "to his credit" tell us about the director?
questions.right: He did the fair thing in the end, though not fully
wrong: He took all the credit himself
He refused to publish the correction
questions.explain: He checked and published a correction, but left out her name.

questions.prompt: What does "barriers" mean in paragraph one?
questions.right: things that stood in the way
questions.explain: Many women faced the same obstacles to becoming scientists.

questions.prompt: Why did Kamala wish her name had been printed?
questions.right: To show later girls that women could do science
wrong: To earn more money from the observatory
To become famous across all of Madras
questions.explain: "I should have liked the girls after me to see that a name like mine could be there."

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say Kamala is invented?
questions.right: To be honest that she is not a real person
wrong: To make the story more exciting
Because her real name is secret
questions.explain: It tells readers that her story represents real women but is not history.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the last paragraph?
questions.right: Many people's work in science went unrecognised
wrong: Old science books are full of mistakes
Historians should not read old records
questions.explain: Their names were left out, but their numbers remain.

texts.title: Debate: Should Marks Be Replaced by Comments?
texts.text:
For the motion — Aditi
Friends, imagine two students. One gets 62 out of 100. The other is told: "Your ideas are original, but your paragraphs need clearer links, and you lost marks by not checking your working." Which student knows what to do next? Marks tell you where you stand; they do not tell you how to move. Worse, they turn learning into a race. Students who score low begin to believe they are "a 40-percent person" and stop trying, while students who score high learn to avoid risks that might cost them a mark. Several schools that have replaced marks with written comments in the middle years report that pupils read their feedback more carefully and redo their work more often. We do not need to abolish standards. We need to describe them in words that help.

Against the motion — Farhan
My opponent describes a lovely comment. But who will write it? A teacher with five classes of forty pupils marks two hundred scripts a week. If every script needs a careful paragraph, either the comments become short and vague — "Good effort, keep it up" — or the teacher stops sleeping. Marks are quick, clear and fair across a whole school. They let a parent see at a glance whether a child is improving, and they let a student compare this term with last. Nothing stops a teacher from giving a mark and two lines of advice. Comments are valuable; they should be added to marks, not replace them. Remove the number, and you remove the one piece of information everyone understands.

questions.prompt: On what point do both speakers agree?
questions.explain: Aditi wants comments; Farhan says comments are valuable but should be added to marks.

questions.prompt: What is Farhan's main practical objection?
questions.right: Teachers lack time to write good comments for everyone
wrong: Comments are unfair to clever students
questions.explain: Two hundred scripts a week would make comments short and vague.

questions.prompt: Why does Aditi open with two imaginary students?
questions.right: To show that a comment tells you what to do next
wrong: To prove that 62 is a good mark
questions.explain: The example makes her argument concrete.

questions.prompt: What does "abolish" mean in Aditi's speech?
questions.explain: "We do not need to abolish standards": not remove them altogether.

questions.prompt: How does Farhan begin his reply?
questions.right: By questioning how her idea would work in practice
wrong: By agreeing with everything she said
By telling a joke about exams
questions.explain: "But who will write it?"

questions.prompt: What is Farhan's final position?
questions.explain: "They should be added to marks, not replace them."

texts.title: Editorial: Homework Should Have Limits
texts.text:
Every evening, in thousands of homes, the same scene plays out. A child sits at the dining table long after dinner, surrounded by notebooks, while a parent wonders whether to help, scold or simply send the child to bed. Homework, once a short reminder of the day's lessons, has grown into a second school day.

Supporters of homework make fair points. Practice fixes skills in the memory. Regular work builds the habit of study, and homework lets parents see what their children are learning. Few would argue that children should never work at home.

The problem is quantity. Studies across several countries suggest that for children under twelve, more than about an hour of homework a night brings little extra benefit, while it eats into sleep, play and family time — all of which matter to learning too. A tired child who has copied answers at ten o'clock has practised nothing except copying.

Schools could fix this without abolishing homework. Teachers in the same class could share one calendar, so that four big tasks do not land on the same night. Homework could be limited by time, not by pages: "work for thirty minutes, then stop" respects children who work slowly. And some homework could simply be reading for pleasure, which research consistently links with success in every subject.

Children are not machines that produce more as we load them more. If we want them to love learning, we must leave them time to live.

questions.prompt: What is the main aim of this editorial?
questions.right: To argue that homework should be limited, not abolished
wrong: To argue that homework should be banned
To praise schools for giving more homework
questions.explain: It accepts homework's value but argues against too much.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer include the supporters' points in paragraph two?
questions.right: To be fair before making the counter-argument
wrong: Because the writer agrees fully with them
To fill space in the newspaper
questions.explain: Admitting fair points makes the argument more convincing.

questions.prompt: What does "has practised nothing except copying" suggest?
questions.right: Too much homework can be useless
questions.explain: A tired child just copies, so no real learning happens.

questions.prompt: Which is one of the writer's suggestions?
questions.right: A shared homework calendar for each class
wrong: No reading at home on weeknights
questions.explain: Teachers could share one calendar so tasks do not pile up.

questions.prompt: "Children are not machines" makes the point that …
questions.right: children cannot simply do more as more is given
questions.explain: Loading a child with work does not keep raising what they produce.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an opinion?
questions.right: We must leave children time to live
wrong: Studies suggest an hour brings most benefit
Reading is linked with success in research
questions.explain: It is the writer's belief; the others report findings.

texts.title: How the Monsoon Works
texts.text:
Every year, usually in the first days of June, the south-west monsoon reaches the coast of Kerala. Over the next six weeks it spreads across almost the whole of India, bringing most of the country's yearly rain in just four months. For farmers, for cities that depend on reservoirs, and for anyone who has stood on a hot roof and smelled the first rain on dry earth, it is the most important weather event of the year. But what actually makes it happen?

The answer begins with the simple fact that land and water heat up differently. In April and May, the sun beats down on the Indian subcontinent and the land becomes very hot. Hot air is lighter, so it rises, leaving an area of low pressure near the ground. Meanwhile, the Indian Ocean warms much more slowly; the air above it stays cooler and heavier, at higher pressure. Air always moves from high pressure towards low pressure, so a great wind begins to blow from the ocean towards the land.

This wind has crossed thousands of kilometres of warm sea, and it is heavy with water vapour. When it reaches the coast and is forced upward — over the Western Ghats, for instance — it cools. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapour, so the vapour condenses into clouds and falls as rain. This is why the western slopes of the Ghats are among the wettest places in India, while the land just behind them, in the "rain shadow", stays much drier.

The monsoon is not perfectly regular. Sometimes it arrives late, or pauses for weeks in what forecasters call a "break". Its strength is affected by conditions far away, including the temperature of the Pacific Ocean. In years of El Niño, when the eastern Pacific becomes unusually warm, the Indian monsoon is often weaker, though not always.

Scientists are also studying how a warming climate is changing the monsoon. Many records suggest that the total rain in a season may not change much, but that it is falling in fewer, heavier bursts, with longer dry spells between them. That matters: a field can use steady rain, but a flood washes soil away, and a long dry spell can ruin young crops.

So the next time the sky darkens in June and the first heavy drops hit the dust, remember that you are watching the end of a journey that began over a distant ocean, driven by nothing more mysterious than the sun, the sea and the land.

questions.prompt: Why does a wind blow from the ocean to the land in summer?
questions.right: The land heats faster, making lower pressure over it
wrong: The ocean is hotter than the land
The Western Ghats push the wind
questions.explain: Air moves from the ocean's higher pressure to the land's low pressure.

questions.prompt: Why does rain fall when the wind rises over the Western Ghats?
questions.right: Rising air cools and its vapour condenses
wrong: Trees on the hills make rain
questions.explain: Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapour.

questions.prompt: What is the "rain shadow"?
wrong: The dark shape of a cloud
Shade under a tree in the rain
questions.explain: The land just behind the Ghats stays much drier.

texts.title: The Girl Who Carried the River
texts.text:
Everyone in Thirumalai village knew the old story. Long ago, the river had refused to come down from the mountain, and the land below was dying. A sage, it was said, caught the whole river in his small water pot and carried it down, step by careful step, so that not one drop was spilled until he reached the fields. Where he finally poured it out, the river had flowed ever since.

Meena had heard this story at every festival of her twelve years. She had also heard, more recently, the district engineer explain that the river was failing again. Sand had been dug from its bed for building, the forest on the mountain had been cut, and in the dry months the river was now a line of stones.

At the village meeting, the men argued about digging a deeper well, about writing to the minister, about whose fault it was. Meena sat at the back and thought about the water pot.

The next morning she walked up the mountain path with her grandmother's brass pot and a bag of seeds. Where the forest had been cleared, the soil was cracking. She dug a small hollow on the slope, pressed in three seeds of the fig trees that used to grow there, and filled the hollow from her pot. Then she walked down, filled the pot at the last pool in the river, and climbed back up to plant three more.

The villagers laughed. "She thinks she is the sage," said the tea-seller. "One pot at a time, she will fix the river in about a thousand years."

But by the end of the week, Meena's two friends were walking up with her. By the end of the month, the schoolteacher had brought her whole class, and the boys who dug sand from the river had been shamed, or paid, into planting instead. Someone built a low wall of stones across a gully so that the rain would soak into the slope rather than racing away. Someone else remembered that their grandfather used to dig small pits along the hillside for the same reason.

The first year, half the seedlings died. The second year, fewer. In the fourth year, the monsoon came, and for the first time anyone could remember, the river was still running when the dry season arrived.

At the next festival, the priest told the old story again: the sage, the pot, the river. When he had finished, a small boy at the front asked, "Was the sage a girl?"

Everyone laughed, and looked at Meena, and Meena looked at her grandmother's pot, which was dented now from four years of mountain paths. "I think," she said, "the pot was the important part. Anyone can carry it."

texts.title: Mother's Hands
texts.text:
I remember them first as weather:
the cool of them on a fevered night,
the quick warm rain of them through my hair
on school mornings, braiding me tight.

They smelled of mustard seed and soap,
of jasmine strung for the evening door;
they could tear a stubborn coconut open
and lift a sleeping child from the floor.

They knew the sums of the household book,
the price of rice, the cost of shoes;
they mended the torn edge of a kurta
so finely the tear became news

that nobody ever heard. They were
never still. Even in the bus
they counted something, folded something,
planned something — mostly us.

Now they are smaller, spotted, slow,
and when I hold them they feel like paper,
like a letter read too many times;
and I read them, and I am grateful.

Poem A — City Morning
The city wakes like a tired giant,
coughing smoke from a thousand throats;
horns argue at every crossing,
and the river carries plastic boats.
Each face in the bus is a closed door;
nobody looks, nobody speaks.
I count the floors of grey towers
and long for the hills of other weeks.

Poem B — My Street at Six
Before the sun, the milkman's bell,
the flower-seller's basket of white;
Mrs Rao waters her doorstep kolam,
the tea-stall kettle sings with light.
The newspaper boy knows every name,
he throws the paper and shouts it too;
our street is a city small enough
to say good morning, and mean it, to you.

texts.title: Review: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind (a book)
texts.text:
Some books tell you a story; this one tells you how a story can change a life.

William Kamkwamba was fourteen when famine struck his village in Malawi. His family could no longer pay his school fees, so he left school. Instead of giving up, he went to the small village library and found a science book with a picture of a windmill on its cover. Using scrap metal, bicycle parts and the frame of a broken bicycle, he built a windmill that brought electricity to his home. Later, he built another to pump water for the fields.

What makes this memoir special is its honesty. William does not pretend that he was a genius from the start. He describes being laughed at by neighbours who thought he had gone mad, the hunger that made it hard to think, and the many failed attempts before the first bulb flickered on. These details make his success feel earned rather than magical.

The book is not perfect. The early chapters about village beliefs move slowly, and some readers may wish for more diagrams of how the windmill actually worked. But these are small complaints.

Read it if you have ever been told that something is impossible. Then, perhaps, go and find a library.

Rating: four and a half stars out of five.

texts.title: From Story to Stage
texts.text:
The story (the opening)
The ferry was late again. Ravi stood on the jetty with his school bag, watching the grey water and counting the minutes. He thought about the test he would miss, and the teacher's raised eyebrow, and his father's quiet disappointment, which was worse than any shout. Behind him, an old woman in a green sari sat on a basket of fish and hummed a song he half remembered from his grandmother's house.

The play (the same scene)
[A jetty. Morning. RAVI, with a school bag, looks at his watch. An OLD WOMAN in a green sari sits on a fish basket.]
RAVI: (to himself) Twenty minutes late. Twenty-one.
OLD WOMAN: (humming, then speaking) Watching the water won't bring the boat, child.
RAVI: I have a test at nine.
OLD WOMAN: And I have fish that won't stay fresh. We each have our worries. (She hums again. RAVI turns, surprised.)
RAVI: That song... my grandmother used to sing it.
OLD WOMAN: Then your grandmother had good taste.

The playwright's note
In the story, readers learn Ravi's fears from his thoughts. On stage, an audience cannot hear thoughts, so I gave the old woman lines that bring his worries out in speech.

texts.title: Why We Should Learn More Than One Language
texts.text:
Friends, I want to begin with a word: "amma". In Tamil it means mother. In Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam it means mother too. Our languages are cousins who share a grandmother, and every time we learn one, we find relatives we did not know we had.

Some say that in a world where English opens so many doors, other languages are a waste of time. I disagree, for three reasons.

First, the brain. Researchers have found that children who learn two or more languages are often better at switching between tasks and at noticing what is important. Learning a language is exercise for the mind, like football is for the legs.

Second, people. A shopkeeper who hears you try a few words of her language will smile at you differently. Language is not just a code for information; it is a way of saying, "You matter to me."

Third, ideas. Some things are said beautifully in one language and clumsily in another. A person with two languages has two windows on the world, and sees more of the view.

Nobody is asking you to become a scholar of ten languages. Learn the language of your neighbour, your grandparents or the state next door. Learn enough to say hello, thank you and sorry. You will be surprised how many doors those three words open.

Thank you.

texts.title: The Signal Box
texts.text:
For thirty-one years, Govindan had worked the signal box at Kallur, a small station where only four trains stopped each day and the rest rushed through without slowing. The box stood on stilts at the end of the platform, with a row of tall iron levers, a brass bell and a window that looked down the line in both directions. Govindan knew every sound the rails made. He could tell a goods train from a passenger train by the hum in the track long before either came round the bend.

The railway had written to him in March. The signals at Kallur would be controlled by computer from the city, two hundred kilometres away. The box would be closed, and Govindan, who was fifty-eight, would retire early. "Nothing personal," the letter said. "Progress."

On his last night, the rain came in sideways. At a quarter past eleven, the bell rang for the Chennai Mail, which would pass at full speed in eighteen minutes. Govindan pulled the levers that set the signals to green, as he had done more than ten thousand times. Then he sat down with his flask of tea and listened.

The rails were wrong.

It was not a sound exactly, more the absence of one. Between the station and the river bridge, where the line ran along an embankment, there should have been a faint ringing as the rain hit the iron. Instead there was a dull, dead patch. Govindan put down his tea. He thought of the landslip twenty years ago, and of how the earth beside the river grew soft in heavy rain.

Every rule told him to trust the instruments, and the instruments showed nothing wrong. If he stopped the Mail without reason, there would be an inquiry, delays across three states and, very likely, a smaller pension. He had eleven minutes.

He threw the signals back to red, rang the station master and ran down the steps with a lantern. The embankment was a quarter of a kilometre away. When he reached it, soaked and gasping, he found that the earth beneath one rail had washed away. The track hung across a gap the size of a lorry, its sleepers swinging gently in the dark like the rungs of a broken ladder.

The Mail stopped at the red signal with a long scream of brakes. Nine hundred passengers slept on, never knowing why they were late.

There was an inquiry after all. It found that the new computer system would not have detected the washout, because the rail itself was unbroken; only the ground beneath it was gone. The report recommended that the Kallur signal box stay open "until further review".

Govindan worked there for two more years. On his real last day, the drivers of every train that passed Kallur gave two long blasts on their horns. He stood at the window and raised his flask to each of them, and when the last one had gone, he sat for a long time and listened to the rails.

texts.title: The Locked Room (two versions)
texts.text:
Telling 1 — told by Nila

I knew something was wrong the moment I reached the top of the stairs. The storeroom door, which Grandfather always kept locked, stood half open, and a thin line of yellow light lay across the dusty floor. Somewhere inside, something scraped slowly against wood. I stopped breathing. The house was empty: Amma had gone to the market, and Grandfather was asleep downstairs. I picked up the umbrella from the stand, though I had no idea what I would do with it, and pushed the door with one finger. It creaked open, inch by inch. In the corner, half hidden behind a trunk, a shape was moving. Then it turned round, and two green eyes caught the light.

Telling 2 — told by the cat

The storeroom smells of old newspapers and mice, and the mice are why I go there. This afternoon the old man forgot to turn the key, so I nosed the door open and slipped in. There is a plump mouse that lives behind the trunk. I had been working at the gap with my paw for some time, scraping and waiting, when the girl came up the stairs. She was breathing like a kettle and holding an umbrella above her head like a stick. I do not know why humans make such a fuss. I turned round to look at her, and she screamed loud enough to warn every mouse in the street. That was the end of my hunt.

What happened next

Nila laughed until she had to sit down on the trunk. The cat, offended, walked out with its tail in the air. Later, when Grandfather heard the story, he said that the scariest things in the world usually turn out to be cats, and the funniest things usually start with someone being afraid.

texts.title: Night on the Backwaters
texts.text:
At dusk the houseboat slid away from the jetty at Alappuzha, and the noise of the town fell behind us like a door closing. The water was so still that every coconut palm along the bank stood twice: once in the air and once, upside down, in the glassy canal.

Our boatman, Joseph, had worked these waters for thirty years. He steered with a long pole, not an engine, and he knew the canals the way a postman knows his streets. "This is a road," he said, pointing at the water. "Children go to school on it. Ducks go to market on it." As if to prove him right, a man paddled past in a narrow canoe, guiding a flock of three hundred ducks with nothing but a stick and a strange, rising whistle.

Night came quickly. Lamps were lit in the houses along the banks, and their reflections wobbled on the black water. Somewhere a radio played an old film song. Frogs began a chorus so loud that we had to raise our voices to talk.

Joseph told us that the backwaters were changing. More boats meant more noise and more fuel in the water; some fish were harder to find, and some fields were sinking under salt water. "The water gives us everything," he said, "so we must give it something back." 

We slept to the knocking of the boat against its rope, and woke to mist and a kingfisher, blue as a struck match, diving where the palms had stood upside down the night before.
